parole.testo: First attested in 1596. Probably from Middle Low German barde + Russian suffix -ыш (-yš).

parole.significato: paper bag for various loose materials
parole.testo: According to Vasmer, from Middle Low German or Low German kartûse, kardûse, from French cartouche.

Inherited from Middle Russian клеверъ (klever), itself borrowed in 16th or 17th c. from Middle Low German klēver, from Proto-West Germanic *klaibrā. Adopted by botanists, displaced local names like Петров крест and дятловина; кашка and трилистник are still occasionally used.
From ку́пор (kúpor, “corkscrew”) + -ить (-itʹ); ку́пор (kúpor) is from Middle Low German kuper (“cooper”), from kupe (“barrel”), from Latin cupa (“barrel”).

parole.significato: idler, slacker, loafer (procrastinating or lazy person)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German lodder (“lack-all, wretch, someone who does not tend to himself”), cognate to Old English loddere (“poorling”). Ukrainian ле́дар (lédar), Czech lotr, Polish łotr.

Borrowed from Middle Low German panser or Polish pancerz, from Middle High German panzier (whence German Panzer). Both German forms stem from Old French pancier, from Latin pantex. The earlier form is пансꙑрь (pansyrʹ).

Inherited from Middle Russian *персикъ (*persik) (derivative персиковъ att. in 17th c.), likely from Middle Low German përsik (equal to Middle High German pfërsich, German Pfersich), from Latin persicum (Latin mālum persicum (fruit), Latin mālus persicus (tree)), see there. Compare Romanian piersic.
Possibly borrowed from Middle Low German pris, from Old French pris, from Latin pretium.

Likely borrowed from Middle Low German rīs, from Late Latin risus, from Latin orīza, oryza, from Ancient Greek ὄρυζα (óruza), ὄρυζον (óruzon); see there for more. Slowly displaced earlier сарацинское пшено during 18th-19th cc.

parole.significato: low shoe (not covering above the ankle)
parole.testo: From the Middle Low German tuffele (compare Low German Tuffel (“shoe”)), from older pantuffel, from French pantoufle (“slipper”). Compare Norwegian and Danish tøffel (“slipper”), Swedish toffel (“slipper”), Latvian tupele.

parole.significato: mine, pit (place from which ore is extracted)

parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Russian аптека (apteka), from Old Ruthenian аптека (apteka), from Middle Polish apteka (16th c.).
